# faa-nasr-airports

**The FAA's airport, heliport and seaplane base list (NASR), for the infrastructure layers**

- **Version recorded:** 2026-10-01
- **Categories:** `emcomm`, `navigation-maps`
- **Upstream:** <https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/aero_data/NASR_Subscription/>

## What it does

Installs one file, the FAA's NASR airport list as CSV in a zip (about 8 MB), under /usr/local/share/hammunition/data/faa-nasr-airports/. Nothing reads it on its own: `hammunition maps infra import --from-nasr` turns the sites in your map regions into a layer for QMapShack, Navit, phones and the browser map, named "Airports and heliports (FAA NASR <cycle>)", each site with its type, status, public or private use, elevation and identifiers.

## Why you would want it

Airfields, hospital heliports and seaplane bases are where people and supplies arrive in a disaster, and where a medevac lands. OpenStreetMap carries many of them (the `transport` layer); the FAA's list is the authoritative one for the US, with every private strip and helipad and its status.

## Before it will work

Map regions installed (`hammunition install osm-regions`): the import keeps what lies in their boxes. QMapShack, Navit or the browser map to see the layer.

## Install and launch

- **Installed by name only** — it is in no profile.
- **Install:** `hammunition install faa-nasr-airports --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Its package ships its own commands and application-menu entry; a unit that ships none gets a generated terminal entry (**D-050**). `hammunition status` lists what is installed.
- **The install needs the network to:** the upstream files the plan lists, each checked against a pinned digest (or, for map and reference data, the publisher or a LAN mirror).

## Offline use

*Not yet documented for this application.* Read “Before it will work” above for what it needs; the install-time network line above is the only offline fact generated from the manifest. Internet, a local network and a radio link are three different things, and this page does not claim any of them works until it says so.

## How it installs

- data (FAA NASR 2026-10-01, public domain, https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/aero_data/NASR_Subscription/): https://nfdc.faa.gov/webContent/28DaySub/extra/01_Oct_2026_APT_CSV.zip (8,030,968 bytes)

## Known problems

US only. A region's box is a rectangle, so it holds sites across a state line. The list is the cycle's: a site closed since is still listed until the pin is regenerated, and a closed one says so in its description. Positions are the FAA's reference points, not runways.

## Keeping it current

- probe: none
- strategy: reinstall
- A new NASR cycle every 28 days. The weekly pin review runs `scripts/gen_nasr_pin.py --check`, which goes red when a newer cycle has taken effect or the pinned URL stops answering; regenerating is running the script with no arguments (an 8 MB download), which writes the new cycle's URL, digest, size, version and licence line into this manifest. The pinned cycle keeps installing as long as the FAA serves it, or from a LAN mirror that holds it.

## Where to get help with the software itself

The FAA's Aeronautical Information Services (https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav/), where a wrong entry is reported; Hammunition only converts the file.
